title: EU leaders seek agreement on long-term budget, Ukraine, ECB leadership despite differences
html:
What you need to know

  • Special European Council meeting for the next two days
  • Details of long-term budget, Ukraine's 2027 financial needs and ECB leadership on the agenda
  • Euro Summit also taking place with outgoing ECB President Christine Lagarde

You can follow developments from the EU summit taking place on Thursday 26th and Friday 27th November below:

Bulgaria ready to back non-military aid for Ukraine

Bulgaria's Prime Minister Rumen Radev said his country would support a proposed €45 billion ($49 billion) EU loan to Ukraine, but only the funds earmarked for non-military aid.

"Bulgaria is going to take part ​in the loan of €20 billion (for) non-military support for Ukraine," ⁠Radev ​told reporters as he arrived ​at the EU summit in Brussels.

"We ​have a ‌huge historic diaspora of Bulgarians living in Ukraine, our wish ​is ⁠to concentrate our support in that area. ⁠We are ​going to contribute, but no money from Bulgaria for weapons," Radev said.

Last week European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the €45 billion would be split into two parts: ‌up to €25 billion for military aid and up to €20 billion for other ‌help as a means of getting member states to contribute where there were objections to funding weapons for Ukraine.

Germany's Merz says EU budget proposal 'still too high'

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that the budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 was "still too too high" and did not provide the basis for an agreement, during comments made as he arrived at the summit.

"After all, the member states must be able ​to afford to pay for ⁠all ​of this," Merz said in Brussels.

​The German leader also said the war in Ukraine needed to be ended as soon as possible and that the country needed help during a "very difficult winter."

Merz said that funding for Kyiv is "a task that we must also accomplish together,” and added: "The European Union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."

Slovakia, the Czech Republic, and Hungary have been exempt from contributing to aid for Ukraine. The countries negotiated, as part of the current €90 billion loan for Ukraine, that they would not have financial obligations in guaranteeing the loan.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis did not agree with the German chancellor.

"Funding for Ukraine should be negotiated separately," said Babis, adding that his country needs the money for other expenditures. "I believe we will fight for this money," providing an early indication of how talks might proceed over the next two days.

European Council chief urges compromise ahead of summit

European Council President Antonio Costa has called on European leaders to seek compromise on the bloc's long-term budget that's up for discussion over the next two days.

"Today as you know we have several points in our agenda, the most important is the approval and the discussion of the next long-term budget for the European Union," Costa said during his doorstop statement.

He said that the budget needed to be "fit to funding our main priorities."

Costa explained that farmers and regions needed support and that there also needed to be more investment in security and defense.

The price of housing and energy also needed to be addressed, Costa said.

Contributions by member states needed to be kept at a "reasonable level" the European Council chief pointed out.

"My objective is to ​bring ‌our leaders closer to a deal," Costa told reporters ahead of the ‌summit in Brussels.

WATCH: Europe's coalition trains for a role in postwar Ukraine

With Ukraine support up for discussion at the two-day summit, Europe remains sidelined in Russia-Ukraine peace talks. But a multinational force is training in Poland to help secure Ukraine and NATO's eastern flank following any future ceasefire.

WATCH: Germany's Merz — Russia wants more than Ukraine

Russia wants more than Ukraine, Germany's chancellor warns. But with a majority of Germans now opposed to military aid for Kyiv, can he make the case that defending Ukraine is in their own interest? Terry Martin speaks to DW Chief Political Editor Michaela Küfner.

READ: EU takes aim at tech giants in tax proposal

European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a smaller EU budget for 2028-2034, including a 3% tax on major digital firms to ease member states' contributions. France has already rejected the plan as inadequate.

European Central Bank leadership also set to be discussed

The Euro Summit will also deal with the process of appointing a new president and two executive board members of the European Central Bank (ECB).

Christine Lagarde has been president since November 2019 but has announced her intention to step down on February 7, 2027.

Eurozone leaders are expected to back Spanish candidate Pablo Hernandez de Cos who is the current head of the Bank for International Settlements.

He's up against Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot for the presidency, while France's Laurence Boone and Germany's Markus Brunnermeier have been nominated for the ECB's two other top jobs.

EU budget from 2028 to 2034 and Ukraine funding on the agenda

European leaders are meeting for the next two days to thrash out a nearly €1.6 trillion ($1.76 trillion) budget proposal for 2028 to 2034.

The 27 member states are hoping to find common ground for a new budget proposal in the coming weeks and for members to agree on it at a summit on December 17 and 18.

"We, collectively, have the responsibility to find a balanced agreement that will allow the European Union to take on the challenges ahead: boosting our competitiveness, strengthening our security and defence and projecting Europe in the world," said President of the European Council Antonio Costa ahead of the talks.

Costa outlined three key objectives for the next two days:

  • to achieve a balanced distribution of funds between the EU's strategic priorities,
  • to keep national contributions within reasonable limits
  • to include a balanced basket of own resources, including five new sources of EU revenue

Revenue would come from digital services, non-recycled e-waste, tobacco related products, the carbon border adjustment mechanism and the emissions trading system, according to a statement from the European Council.

Ukraine's financing needs for 2027 and beyond will also be dealt with during talks. Currently, €45 billion has been earmarked in additional financial support for Ukraine in 2027, building on the EU's €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan for 2026 and 2027.

It's not expected to be a smooth process with Reuters quoting a diplomat as expecting "leaders to be yelling, complaining, showing they are willing to fight. They need that ​first. They need a breakdown, blood on the walls, before they can get to an agreement."

Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to DW's coverage of the two-day Special European Council meeting in Brussels, which is expected to focus on the EU’s next long-term budget, support for Ukraine and then the leadership of the European Central Bank (ECB).

Leaders of the bloc's 27 members states will be looking to find common ground over the budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 ahead of an expected deal in December.

Continued support for Ukraine in 2027 and beyond is up for discussion as Russia's invasion drags on towards a fifth year.

The question of who replaces European Central Bank chief Christine Lagarde is also on the agenda.

Follow here for the latest developments from the two-day talks.
summary: Leaders of the EU's 27 member states are expected to thrash out the EU's budget for 2028 to 2034. Ukraine and European Central Bank leadership are also up for discussion. DW has more.
